The National Pension Commission has called on the private sector to contribute to the sustainability of the Federal Government’s ₦52,500 minimum monthly pension for low-income retirees, disclosing that the government and pension industry have so far provided ₦400bn to the Pension Protection Fund. The Director-General of PenCom, Omolola Oloworaran, said the pension industry contributed ₦50bn, while the Federal Government provided ₦350bn, including payments to clear outstanding pension backlogs. Speaking during an interview with ARISE NEWS on Monday, Oloworaran said wider private-sector participation was necessary to sustain the initiative and guarantee financial security for vulnerable retirees. She said, “But in order for this to be sustainable, so that we can continue to support a minimum pension and ensure that vulnerable Nigerians have security in old age, the private sector must come through. And as of today, the industry has contributed 50 billion, the federal government another 350 billion, because they went and paid all the backlog.” Oloworaran explained that PenCom had engaged an actuary to assess the financial implications of the initiative and project its long-term sustainability. She said the minimum pension arrangement would also be reviewed in line with inflation and the available funding. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. She expressed confidence that the current funding could sustain the initiative for at least 10 years based on existing projections. “Conservatively, we’re good for the next 10 years. Conservatively,” she said. The PenCom boss disclosed that 54 per cent of beneficiaries who had received payments under the initiative were private-sector retirees. She added that nearly 70 per cent of workers expected to qualify for the programme were in the private sector. PenCom disputes claims of unpaid federal pensions dating back to 2004 On complaints about unpaid federal pensions, Oloworaran disputed claims that some retirees who left service in 2004 and 2005 were still owed their entitlements. She explained that retirees who left service before the introduction of the Contributory Pension Scheme in 2007 were covered by the Defined Benefit Scheme, which is managed by the Pension Transitional Arrangement Directorate, rather than PenCom. “I vehemently stand by what I’m saying. That under the contributory pension scheme, you don’t have anybody owed that much. Even PTAD as well, nothing,” she said. However, she acknowledged that pension payments remained a challenge in some states, noting that only 14 of the 36 states were paying pensions regularly. “We have 14 states that are paying up. But 14 out of 36 states is a lot. And some states are doing very badly,” she said. Oloworaran also discussed the PenCare Health Initiative, which provides eligible retirees with access to healthcare services. She said beneficiaries would enrol through their Pension Fund Administrators, adding that the scheme currently covered one general health check annually but did not include major operations or serious illnesses. “What we are doing is setting aside a critical illness fund so that people can use that. Of course, that will then have a limit. If it runs out, we won’t be able to pay for it,” she said. The PenCom DG said the commission was also working to ensure that retirees received additional support through the initiative.
